newsitem.title: CHINA: China's interbank market small but growing.
newsitem.headline: China's interbank market small but growing.

text.p: China's one-year-old local currency interbank market has opened a channel for free movement of the Chinese yuan and allowed interest rates to be market-driven for the first time, analysts said on Friday.

But the market, which began trial operations on January 1, is still limited in its scope compared to other major financial markets, with Beijing restricting the number of members and many firms still forced to borrow money on the black market.
"With the opening of the interbank market, surplus money of Chinese financial institutions can now freely flow for the first time," said one official with the People's Bank of China.
Once the market opened, member banks could borrow and lend short-term money amongst themselves.
"The market's rates have been the only free interest rates in China based on demand and supply after the cancellation of a ceiling system in June," the central bank official said.
On June 1, the central bank liberalised the rates on the market by abolishing daily limits on how much rates could move up or down in a day.
Before the market was set up, only the central bank could decide short-term money flows among state-run commercial banks.
It did this mainly on the basis of the banks' financial reports, which lagged far behind real supply and demand conditions in the market place, banking analysts said.

The money and rate movements on the interbank market also provide the central bank with valuable statistics, which it uses to adjust monetary policy, the analysts said. But interest rates outside the market remain controlled by the central bank.

Beijing has ordered that money borrowed on the market be exclusively used for working capital and not for investment in fixed assets, securities trading, real estate speculation or purchase of company shares.
"The market is still very small, with the central government barring most financial institutions from trading directly," said a banker with the Shanghai-based Bank of Communications.
"This means that the market rates cannot fully reflect China's national money supply picture."

In the first 10 months of trading, total turnover on interbank market was 470 billion yuan ($56.63 billion), compared with more than 600 billion yuan in stock trading and over 1.3 trillion yuan in treasury bill trading in the same period on the Shanghai stock market.
At present, only the head offices of 19 major Chinese banks and 35 short-term financial centres, money brokerages run by the People's Bank of China, can trade on the interbank market.

Other banks, bank branches, hundreds of other short-term financial centres run by state commercial banks, securities and futures brokerages and company finance departments cannot trade directly and have to go through members of the market.
Bankers said the small market turnover caused many surplus short-term funds to flow among financial institutions through black market trading, leading to many irregularities.

"It is very difficult to get quick money from the interbank market," said an executive with a major Chinese securities house. "This has made us resort more to the treasury bill markets for short-term money." ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
